title: Vom Bonner Judengasse zum Rheinischen Bankhaus — Bonn to Cologne
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Die Bonner Judengasse — Blood of the Court-Jews

stops.name: Bonn, Judengasse — the birth
stops.campa: In the narrow Judengasse of Bonn, the electoral residence-town on the Rhine, Salomon is born on 19 June to Herz Salomon Oppenheim, a small merchant, and Helene née Seligmann. The house stands within the walls that pen the Jews of the Prince-Archbishop of Cologne; four generations of Oppenheims have served that court as moneylenders and purveyors, honoured and never free. The child inherits a name already heavy with credit and grievance. Outside the ghetto gate the electoral palace glitters; inside, the ledgers are kept, the loans advanced, the taxes borne. He is born into the trade of standing near power without holding it.

stops.name: The electoral court of Max Franz — the inherited patronage
stops.campa: Maximilian Franz of Austria, youngest son of the Empress Maria Theresa, takes the electoral throne of Cologne and makes his Bonn residence a small enlightened capital. To this court the Oppenheims are bound as Hoffaktoren — court-factors who procure luxuries, provisions and silver for the prince and advance him money against his revenues. The boy Salomon grows up in the shadow of this dependency, learning that a merchant Jew may be indispensable and still forbidden the city walls of Cologne downstream, closed to his people since 1424. The lesson takes: serve the court, but build something that outlasts it.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Elector Maximilian Franz of Austria

stops.name: Bonn — friendship with the young Beethoven
stops.campa: In the same Bonn of the same years, a court organist's son of like age plays before the Elector: Ludwig van Beethoven. Salomon knows him; the acquaintance ripens into a friendship the canon records as lifelong. Two Rhinelanders of 1770 and 1772, the one to command the world's ears, the other its Rhenish credit — they meet in the theatre boxes and music-rooms of the electoral town. Years hence, when Beethoven is deaf and glorious in Vienna, the Cologne banker remains among the friends of his youth, a thread of art laid across the thread of money.

stops.name: Bonn — the merchant father's small trade
stops.campa: The father Herz Salomon Oppenheim keeps a small merchant's trade in the Bonn Judengasse, never grown rich, a purveyor and moneylender in the electoral town. From him the son learns the whole grammar of the business: the weighing of a bill, the trust that is a merchant's only capital, the art of standing surety. It is a modest counter, and the boy has already outgrown it in ambition. The next year the father will stake his own son in a house of the son's founding — the small trade of the ghetto lane breeding the great house of the century. Everything begins from this narrow counter.

segments.name: Die Gründung — A House at Seventeen

stops.name: Bonn — the founding of the commission-and-exchange house
stops.campa: At seventeen, in the very year the Bastille falls in Paris, Salomon Oppenheim sets up his own house in Bonn — a commission-and-exchange business, dealing in goods and in bills of drawn money. His father Herz Salomon stakes the first capital; a silent partner, Samuel Wolff, adds his. Wine and oil and cotton move through the young firm; foreign coin is changed, credit advanced, freight forwarded. Across the Rhine an old order burns; here a new order is quietly opened as a ledger. The date on the first entries is 1789. The house that will endure two centuries begins as a boy's account-book.

stops.name: Dülmen / Bonn — the marriage to Therese Stein
stops.campa: In 1792 Salomon marries Deigen Levi of Dülmen — soon called Therese Stein — daughter of a Westphalian merchant. She brings a dowry of ten thousand talers into the young house, and more: a head for the trade equal to his own. She will bear twelve children and sit beside him in the counting-room, advising, deciding, a partner in all but the name over the door. The wars will make and unmake fortunes around them; through every reversal Therese steadies the capital. In her the house gains not a wife only but its second founder, the woman who will one day command it in her own signature.

stops.name: The left bank falls — French troops on the Rhine
stops.campa: The armies of the Republic cross the Rhineland; the electorate of Max Franz collapses, its prince a fugitive, and the whole left bank passes under France. With the old order fall the old walls — and the four-century ban that shut the Jews out of Cologne is void, for the Republic decrees the freedom of religions. What the Enlightenment could not grant the Jews of the Rhine, the sword of the Revolution now imposes. Salomon reads the map with a merchant's eye: Bonn is a residence without a court; Cologne downstream is the free port of German banking, and its gates now stand open to him.

segments.name: Der Zug nach Köln — Into the Forbidden City

stops.name: Cologne — the move, and the reopening of a Jewish city
stops.campa: In 1798 Salomon Oppenheim moves his house from Bonn to Cologne — and by that act becomes one of the founders of a Jewish community there after four hundred and twenty-four years of exile. Where his fathers were forbidden even to lodge, the son now sets up his counting-house and his hearth. It is the first great turning: the boy of the Bonn ghetto walks free through gates that once would have arrested him. The Republic's law made it possible; his own nerve makes it real. Cologne is the banking metropolis of the German lands, and he has come to take his place in it.

stops.name: Cologne — the rented house of the vinegar-maker Hahn
stops.campa: The first Cologne residence is a house rented from the vinegar-manufacturer G. J. Hahn, held from 1801 to 1808. From these rooms the firm trades under French law as a house of standing; the bills of Cologne, Frankfurt and Amsterdam pass across its desks. Colonial wares, wine, oil and cotton still move as goods; but more and more the business is money itself — discount, exchange, credit. In a handful of years the newcomer from Bonn is climbing the ranks of a city crowded with old commercial dynasties. He is patient, he is exact, and he is building toward a house of his own.
suggested_refs: Sal. Oppenheim jr. & Cie. company history

stops.name: Cologne — Napoleon enters the city, 13 September 1804
stops.campa: The Emperor comes to the Rhine. On 13 September 1804 Napoleon and Josephine enter Cologne through the Eigelstein gate, and the merchant city stages its homage — arches, illuminations, silver medals for diligent scholars. For a Jew of Cologne the sight is charged: this is the power whose law made him a citizen and let him through these very walls. The Code that bears the Emperor's name guarantees, on the left bank, the civic rights of his people. Under this régime the house of Oppenheim will be classed, in the French registers, as Banquier et Négociant Notable — a notable banker and merchant of the imperial city.
suggested_refs: Napoleon's entry into Cologne 1804, contemporary prints

stops.name: Cologne — the classical house at Große Budengasse 8
stops.campa: In January 1808 Salomon Oppenheim buys the patrician house at Große Budengasse 8 — a classical mansion raised in 1780 for the banker Jakob Pelzer. He is no longer a tenant but a proprietor in the heart of the banking quarter, and the address becomes the seat of the house for a generation. Under the Empire's registers he stands as a Banquier notable; in the counting-rooms of this Pelzer mansion the discounts of the Rhine are set. The boy from the Bonn Judengasse now keeps his ledgers in one of Cologne's finest merchant palaces. The house has arrived where it meant to stand.

segments.name: Die Kontinentalsperre — Fortunes Made in the Blockade

stops.name: Cologne — the Continental System and the commodity fortunes
stops.campa: The Emperor seals the Continent against English trade, and the price of every smuggled or scarce ware — cotton, colonial sugar, coffee, indigo — leaps and lurches. In this fever of blockade and scarcity a nimble house of commodities and bills can make fortunes, and Oppenheim makes his. By 1810 he stands as the second banker of Cologne, behind only Abraham Schaaffhausen. The wars that ruin princes enrich the discounters who can move goods and credit across shifting frontiers. The firm passes from a trader's house into a true banking house, its capital swollen by the very disorder of the age.

stops.name: Cologne — the sons growing into the house
stops.campa: In the Cologne years the heirs grow who will carry the house into its dynasty. Simon, born in 1803, and Abraham, born in 1804, are children now at the Große Budengasse; Dagobert follows, and among the daughters Betty, who will marry into the Hertz line that gives the world the physicist of the electric wave. Twelve children fill the house. Salomon and Therese are raising not merely a family but a succession — a house of Oppenheim meant to stand when its founder is gone. The father will train the sons at the ledger as his own father trained him; the trade descends, generation to generation.
suggested_refs: Portraits of Simon and Abraham Oppenheim

stops.name: Aachen and Frankfurt — the arteries of the bill-trade
stops.campa: The house lives by its correspondents. Bills drawn on Frankfurt, on Amsterdam, on Aachen and Paris cross Oppenheim's desks and are discounted, remitted, protested, renewed; the credit of the Rhine flows through this web of paper. Aachen, the old coronation city, and Frankfurt, the fair and money capital, are the poles between which Cologne's exchange swings. In an age when a courier's week decides a fortune, the banker who knows the true rate on every square keeps the advantage. Oppenheim keeps it. The firm's name becomes good on paper in every market that matters, from the North Sea to the Main.

stops.name: Vienna — the Congress and the shrinking of the promise
stops.campa: At Vienna the powers redraw Europe, and the Rhineland is given to Prussia. For the Jews of the German lands the Congress is a reversal: the rights the Code Napoleon granted them are now hedged, disputed by the restored order of the Holy Alliance. What the Revolution opened, the Restoration would half-close. Oppenheim, made a citizen under France, wakes a Prussian subject under a crown that must still be argued with for his equality. The great fortune is secure; the great question — whether a Jew of the Rhine is a full citizen or a tolerated guest — is thrown open again.

stops.name: Cologne to Berlin — the transfer of the French war indemnity
stops.campa: Prussia is owed the war indemnity of a defeated France, and the moving of that vast sum from Paris to Berlin is a task for the surest houses. Oppenheim, together with the Mendelssohn bank of Berlin, organises the transfer — the discounted bills, the remittances, the great flows of coin and paper marshalled across a continent. The Jewish banker of Cologne now serves the Prussian state at the highest reach of its finance, indispensable to the crown that still withholds his full citizenship. The paradox of the Court-Jew, inherited from his fathers, is played out on a European scale: trusted with the treasury, denied the franchise.

stops.name: Cologne — Therese granted the signature that spans nations
stops.campa: In 1821 Therese Oppenheim is granted Wechselfähigkeit — the capacity of the bill. From this year a document bearing her signature can draw money in many countries; her name alone commands credit across the frontiers of Europe. It is an extraordinary grant to a woman of the age, and it seals what was already true: she is the co-sovereign of the house. Salomon's health is uncertain; the succession must be sure. With her signature made good in every market, Therese stands ready to hold the firm should its founder fall. The partnership begun with a Dülmen dowry now reaches its full and public authority.

segments.name: Ehre und Emanzipation — Honours Withheld and Won

stops.name: Cologne — Royal Prussian Court Agent, January 1822
stops.campa: In 1822 the Prussian crown names Salomon Oppenheim Königlich Preußischer Oberhofagent — Royal Prussian High Court Agent — rewarding his service to the treasury. The old title of his Bonn fathers, borne once toward a prince-archbishop, is now conferred by a king of Prussia. It is honour and irony together: the Court-Jew tradition he was born into, which Samuel Oppenheimer and Joseph Süß Oppenheimer had lived and died within, descends to him renewed. He has transcended their fate — no fall of a patron ruins him — yet he wears their very style. The banker of the free market is decorated in the language of the old dependency.

stops.name: Cologne — first Jew in the Chamber of Commerce
stops.campa: In 1822 Salomon Oppenheim is elected to the Chamber of Commerce of Cologne — the first Jew ever seated in that body. A merchant guild that a generation before would not have let his people through the city gate now takes him into its council. The honour is real and it is a breach in the wall: by his standing, his reliability, his sheer weight in the trade of the Rhine, he has forced open a door for those who come after. Emancipation is not decreed here; it is earned, seat by seat, ledger by ledger. The Court-Jew's grandson sits among the free merchants of Cologne as an equal.
suggested_refs: Cologne Chamber of Commerce, historical membership

stops.name: Cologne — facing the shades of the Court-Jews
stops.campa: In his honour Salomon Oppenheim answers the shades of his kind. Behind him stand the great Court-Jews: Samuel Oppenheimer, who financed the Emperor's wars against the Turk and died with the treasury owing him millions it would not pay; Joseph Süß Oppenheimer, hanged at Stuttgart in an iron cage when his prince died and his enemies fell upon him. Their fate was the fate of the factor whose whole fortune hung on one master's life. Salomon has broken that fate. His house rests not on a single prince but on the market itself; when kings fall, his ledgers stand. He inherits the Court-Jew's craft and transcends the Court-Jew's doom.

segments.name: Dampf und Eisen — The Machine Age Financed

stops.name: Cologne — the Prussian-Rhenish Steamship Company on the Rhine
stops.campa: The age of steam comes to the Rhine, and Oppenheim is among the first to found it in shares. He helps raise the Prussian-Rhenish Steamship Company — the ancestor of the Cologne–Düsseldorf line — putting the joint-stock company to work upon the river that made his fortune. Where his house once forwarded freight in sailing barges, it now sets steamers churning against the current between the Rhenish towns. This is the pivot from the old commerce to the new industry: the banker becomes the founder, the Gründer, whose capital calls machines into being. The river of his boyhood is remade by the money he has gathered on its banks.

stops.name: Cologne — insurance and the seeds of the industrial house
stops.campa: In the last years of the founder, the house reaches into transport insurance and the founding of enterprises — the assurance of goods on river and road, the participations that anticipate the railways and mines his sons will bankroll. Salomon lays the pattern: a private bank that does not merely lend but conceives, floats and holds the industries of a modernising Rhineland. The Ruhr coal, the Aachen works, the iron roads not yet laid — all are foreshadowed in these ventures. He will not live to see the empire of Rhenish industry his house will finance, but he draws its first plans in the 1820s.

segments.name: Der Tod und die Dynastie — The House Passes On

stops.name: Mainz — the death of the founder, 8 November 1828
stops.campa: On 8 November 1828 Salomon Oppenheim dies at Mainz, upon the Rhine that was the whole road of his life — born at Bonn, risen at Cologne, ended at the river's Hessian bend. Fifty-six years carried him from the ghetto lane to the first bench of German banking, from a boy's ledger of 1789 to a house that clears the treasuries of kings. He dies a Court Agent of Prussia, a member of the Chamber of Commerce, the founder of a fortune that will outlast dynasties of princes. The Rhine that bore his barges and his steamers now bears his death; the house he raised does not die with him.

stops.name: Deutz — burial in the Jewish cemetery across the Rhine
stops.campa: He is brought to rest among his people at the Jewish cemetery of Deutz, on the right bank facing the Cologne he opened to the Jews. The community he helped refound after four centuries of exile receives its founder into its ground. From this bank of the river the cathedral towers stand across the water — the city that once shut its gates to his fathers, now the seat of the house that bears his name. The Court-Jew of the old style is buried as a free man of the new, in a city that Jews were forbidden to enter within his own grandfather's memory.

stops.name: Cologne — Therese and the sons take the house forward
stops.campa: With the founder gone, Therese Oppenheim takes up the direction of the house at the side of her sons Simon and Abraham. The widow whose signature already commands credit in many nations now governs a great bank — a woman at the head of Rhenish finance, unheard of in her time. Under her hand and her sons', the house will pour its capital into railways, mines, insurance and heavy industry, raising the Rhineland's machine age. From the Bonn ghetto to a two-century dynasty of Rhenish banking, the line holds. The founder's ledger of 1789 has become an inheritance; the house of Oppenheim enters the age its founder foresaw.
